app.title: Spectral Panel Picker
app.summary: The person lists the markers in their experiment, picks the dyes they have on hand for each one, and ticks the markers that matter most. The app searches every combination of one dye per marker with no dye used twice. It ranks the panels so that the most similar pair of dyes is as different as possible, considering key markers first, then the whole panel, then a complexity index. The person opens any ranked panel to see its pairwise similarity matrix, its most similar pairs and its dye signatures, and downloads the ranked table. A second tab runs the same check on a panel the person already has.

task.text: Choose one dye per marker for a spectral flow cytometry panel so that the dyes stay as easy to unmix as possible, and check an existing panel for pairs that are too close.

data.text: Reference spectral signatures, one row per dye and one column per detector, either simulated from public excitation and emission spectra or uploaded from single-stain controls. The person adds a list of markers, each with the dyes available for it.
data.item: a candidate panel assigning one dye to each marker

stage.text: planning a cytometry panel before staining and acquisition

mechanism.text: A form of marker rows with dye multi-selects and key checkboxes feeds a combinatorial search. The search fills a ranked table of panels, and choosing a panel from that table draws its similarity heatmap, its worst-pairs list, its complexity metric and a line chart of its signatures. A check tab sends a hand-picked dye set to the same detail view.

field.text: fluorochrome panel design for spectral flow cytometry in immunology

workflow.name: choose one option per slot from candidate lists to minimise the worst conflict

steps.here: Built-in signatures are simulated from public dye spectra for the instrument's lasers. A sidebar uploader can replace them with a CSV of the person's own reference signatures, normalised per dye.

steps.step: list the slots and the candidates available for each, marking which slots matter most
steps.here: A number input sets how many markers there are. Each marker row has a name, a multi-select of the dyes on hand and a 'key' checkbox, and the rows are seeded with an example panel.

steps.step: compute a value from the data
steps.here: 'Find panels' runs a pruned depth-first search over one-dye-per-marker combinations with no dye reused. Panels are scored by the worst cosine similarity among key-marker pairs, then among all pairs, then by the condition number. The button warns when a marker has no dyes and when the search stops early.

steps.step: look over every item at a glance
steps.here: A 'Best panels' table shows the top 10 ranked panels with key pairs max, all pairs max, complexity and the dye chosen for each marker.

'Look at panel' selects a ranked panel and shows a similarity heatmap, the complexity index, the five most similar pairs coloured by hard-to-unmix thresholds, and a line chart of each dye's signature across detectors.
'Download table' saves the ranked panels as panels.csv.

steps.step: check an existing selection for conflicts
steps.here: The 'Check a panel' tab takes any set of dyes picked by hand and sends it to the same heatmap, worst-pairs and signature view.

distinctive: Each candidate is ranked by its single worst pair (a minimax objective) rather than by an average, and pairs involving priority slots are ranked first.
A conditioning measure (the condition number of the signature matrix) breaks ties as an overall index of unmixing difficulty.
Fixed similarity thresholds (0.98 and 0.90) colour pairs as very hard to unmix or as needing care.
The search is pruned and has a step limit, and the person is told when it stopped early and the result may not be optimal.
Reference signatures are simulated from excitation times binned emission for each instrument laser, and the person can swap in measured single-stain controls.
